parts.title: Many-way light interference with any kind of light-splitting device, including ones that lose some light
parts.abstract:
When two photons (the tiny particles that make up light) meet, they can affect each other in surprising ways. One of the most important tools for studying this is quantum interferometry: sending light through a network of beam splitters and watching how the photons interfere with one another. It makes possible many kinds of quantum information technology that go beyond what classical physics allows. Most of this work has used "unitary" devices, which are lossless and keep the number of photons the same. These are described by square tables of numbers, called N × N matrices. Some devices, however, lose some light on the way. They are described by rectangular tables, called m × n matrices, and they need a different approach.

In this paper, we show in an experiment a simple but powerful tool for uncovering the basic features of many-way light interference with these lossy devices. To check their interesting unitary and nonunitary properties, we used Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference. This is the well-known effect in which two identical photons arriving at the same time at opposite sides of a beam splitter end up together at one output. It reveals a hidden "exchange phase", a kind of sign that changes when the two photons swap places. With our device, we can easily use both the usual HOM interference, which comes from unitary devices, and an unusual version, which comes from nonunitary ones.

These results offer another way to study how light and matter interact at the quantum level. They also make it easier to use complex many-way light interference for large-scale quantum information tasks, such as quantum simulation and quantum computing.
parts.introduction_first:
Quantum interference is when the waves of particles add up or cancel out in ways that classical physics cannot explain. Making use of it promises to make many kinds of quantum technology work better, beyond what classical physics allows. Examples include very precise sensors (1, 2), long-distance communication that is secure by nature (3–5), and, for certain tasks, computers that are exponentially faster than classical ones (6, 7).

A classic example of this kind of effect is Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference. Picture a beam splitter, a device that splits a beam of light into two paths. Now send two identical photons in at the same time, one from each side. They end up together at one of the two outputs. This happens directly because photons are bosons, a type of particle that likes to share the same state, and because a lossless beam splitter is unitary, meaning it keeps the number of photons the same (8–10).

Quantum technologies aim to speed things up in many areas, so they need complex circuits with many inputs and outputs (11, 12). In the experimental setups that exist today, people routinely model and use unitary transformations when they process information with light. These keep the number of photons the same and follow the rules that bosons obey. They are built from two simple parts: a phase shifter, which adds a delay to one path, and a lossless beam splitter, which mixes two paths. Because of this, any unitary transformation can be carried out step by step, following a recipe.

However, the unitary rule limits what a transformation table can look like. Nonunitary transformations may loosen these limits and open up exciting chances to carry out any transformation we want.
parts.introduction_rest:
Some problems are so hard that no one knows how to solve them with a computer in a reasonable time. Scientists call these "NP-complete" problems. Solving them with only unitary devices may not be possible, so nonunitary devices could offer another way (13, 14).

Nonunitary devices are already useful in real-world physics. Some physical systems are "open", which means they are not sealed off from their surroundings. As time passes, they lose some of their energy or information. Nonunitary devices help us model how these systems interact with the real world around them, and with the small flaws that every real optical part has (15).

Nonunitary devices also help protect delicate quantum states. Quantum entanglement, where two or more particles become linked so that they behave as one, is fragile. It is easily disturbed by "decoherence", the way a quantum system slowly leaks information into its surroundings and loses its special quantum behavior. Researchers have therefore developed a way to filter out the entanglement in light using nonunitary optics. This reduces the harmful contact between the quantum system and its surroundings (16).

There is another reason to go beyond unitary networks. A transformation may have a different number of input paths and output paths that we care about. That is a clear sign that it is nonunitary (17). Nonunitary transformations also have one more useful feature: they let us tune quantum interference very finely. This matters for two kinds of tasks. The first is Boson sampling, where many photons are sent through a network and we record where they end up. The second is quantum walks, where a particle takes random steps through a network. With nonunitary transformations, both tasks may be able to copy the behavior of fermions, particles that avoid sharing the same state, or of anyons, particles that behave differently from both. Such behavior can be directly imitated by many-way light interference in networks whose settings can be changed (12, 18).

So far, experiments with these unitary operations have mostly used 2 × 2 transformation tables, which act on two paths. Many kinds of lossy beam splitters have been studied in depth and have shown many interesting effects. They include beam splitters based on graphene (19, 20), metasurfaces (21), surface plasmon polaritons (22), thin films of chromium, silicon nitride and chromium (Cr-SiN-Cr) (23), and fully integrated waveguides with carefully designed light loss (24).

However, many-way light interference with any kind of nonunitary transformation is essential for large-scale quantum information processing. Programmable quantum chips need this especially badly, because they must be able to control their quantum operations as they run. Until now, this problem has only been studied in theory, through the idea of carrying out any linear transformation. That idea gives a clever way to break any desired operation down into smaller pieces (17, 25). As a result, many-way light interference with any kind of nonunitary transformation has not yet been explored, especially as a way to make programmable chips that handle light.

In this paper, we show that any many-way light interference with any kind of nonunitary transformation can be taken from a unitary circuit made of light (17, 26). Any unitary operation with a fixed number of paths can, in theory, be designed and built in the lab by breaking it down into simple building blocks (27, 28). This means that any kind of nonunitary operation can be achieved in a short and efficient way.

The circuit also lets us adjust two things: the phase shifts, which add delays to the light, and the mixing between paths. With these, we can precisely control each number in the transformation table. This opens the door to using complex unitary and nonunitary operations that are needed in programmable integrated optics, where light is processed on a single chip.

We build on two ideas: the way a nonunitary operation can be "dilated", or expanded, into a larger unitary one, and the fact that any unitary operation with a fixed number of paths can be carried out. Using balanced beam splitters, which split light equally between two paths, we build a 4 × 4 unitary transformation. Inside it sits a smaller 2 × 2 transformation, and we can switch on and off its unitary property as we choose.

We also want to confirm an interesting effect: the exchange phase, the sign that changes when two photons swap places, behaves differently in unitary and nonunitary transformations. To test this, we send pairs of photons into the 4 × 4 circuit from different input paths. Whether the two photons end up together at one output (coalescence) or apart (anticoalescence) is decided by the smaller 2 × 2 operation. This finely tunable many-way light interference may offer another way to control how photons affect each other. That, in turn, could give a very flexible tool for large-scale and complex quantum technologies.

This work confirms a promising approach: using carefully designed unitary circuits to produce any nonunitary transformation we want. It also lays the groundwork for advanced quantum technologies built on programmable chips that handle light. We expect that adding these nonunitary transformations to quantum information processing would greatly expand the range of quantum operations and tasks that integrated light chips can do. For example, our method lets us build nonunitary transformations that act on many paths at once, for interference between many photons. This may offer another route to building various quantum logic gates, the basic operations of a quantum computer, in experiments (14, 29, 30).
parts.methods:
## Materials and methods

To make our experiment, we used a laser diode, a small laser that gives off a steady, continuous beam of light at a wavelength of 405 nanometres (nm). A grating, a tiny ruled surface, holds the laser's colour very precisely. We shone this beam into two crystals, each 2 mm long, made of a material called potassium titanyl phosphate. The crystals are "type II" and "periodically poled", which means they are built in layers that switch the way they handle light, so that they can turn one colour of light into two others. We placed the two crystals at right angles to each other.

Inside each crystal, the laser light (the "pump") splits into two new photons, called the "signal" and the "idler". This process is called spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC). The crystals are set up so that the pump, signal and idler all travel along the same line, a condition called type II collinear phase matching. At a temperature of 23.5°C, the pump light has a centre wavelength of about 405 nm, and the signal and idler each have a centre wavelength of about 810 nm.

Light waves can vibrate in different directions, and this is called their polarization. We used two thin plates in the pump beam, a half-wave plate and a quarter-wave plate, to set its polarization at a diagonal angle. A phase shifter that we could adjust then added a controllable delay, ϕω, between the two parts of the beam. The polarization of the incoming light was therefore (∣Hp〉+exp(iϕω)∣Vp〉)/2. This made sure that both crystals, which sit at right angles to each other, received the same amount of pump light.

As a result, the first crystal turned horizontally polarized pump light (∣Hp〉) into a pair of photons, one horizontal and one vertical (∣Hω1Vω2〉). The second crystal turned vertically polarized pump light (∣Vp〉) into a pair with the opposite arrangement, one vertical and one horizontal (∣Vω1Hω2〉). Here H and V stand for horizontal and vertical polarization. A polarization beam splitter then sent the two polarization states along separate paths. The combined quantum state of the two pairs can be written as ∣Ψ〉=(∣ω1ω2〉+exp(iϕω)∣ω2ω1〉)/2.

We could adjust two things continuously by changing the temperature at which the crystals work, called the phase matching temperature. The first is the frequency detuning, Δ=∣ω1−ω2∣, which is how far apart the two photons' frequencies are. The second is the relative phase, ϕω, which is the delay between them. At 23.5°C, the detuning is Δ=0 THz (terahertz, a unit of frequency). The two photons then have the same wavelength, and the entanglement is symmetric. At 42°C, the detuning reaches Δ=2.2 THz and the phase is ϕω=π. The two photons now have different wavelengths, and the entanglement is antisymmetric. At 60°C, the detuning reaches Δ=4.2 THz and the phase is ϕω=0. The photons again have different wavelengths, but the entanglement is symmetric.

Next, we sent these photons, whether their frequencies were matched or not, into single-mode optical fibres. These are thin glass fibres that carry only one kind of light pattern, called the Gaussian mode, so that only this pattern could travel into the 4 × 4 quantum interferometry from each of the different input ports. We used four single-photon detectors, labelled A, B, C and D, to measure how likely the photons were to appear at each of the four output ports.

The paired photons were detected by silicon avalanche photon diodes, which are very sensitive detectors that click when a single photon arrives. A fast electronic AND gate counted a pair as a "coincidence" when both photons reached their detectors within a coincidence time window of 1 ns (one billionth of a second). This let us study the coincidence events for every possible pair of detectors, AB, AC, AD, BC, BD and CD.
parts.results:
## Results

We start by describing the basic idea for carrying out any nonunitary transformation table, Tm×n, as shown in Fig. 1. A rectangular table like this has m rows and n columns. In our setup, m is the number of input paths (or "modes") and n is the number of output paths.

To see why this matters, it helps to know about a special kind of square table called a complex Hadamard matrix. It links the standard set of states that a quantum computer uses, called the computational basis, to another set of states that is "mutually unbiased" with it. In other words, the two sets are so different that knowing which state a particle is in one set tells you nothing about which state it is in the other.

Because of this, Tm×n can be thought of as a device with m inputs and n outputs. Very few experiments have actually built such devices. To solve this problem, we use a mathematical trick called matrix dilation (17). It turns the nonunitary table Tm×n into a larger unitary table, SN×N. Here N is the number of input and output paths, and N is at least n and at least m.

Any unitary device with many inputs and outputs can be built from a different arrangement of beam splitters and phase shifters. The best designs for these have already been studied in detail (27, 28). So the methods already developed for lossless N × N devices can now be used to carry out any m × n nonunitary transformation.

For example, any m × n linear transformation with m ≤ n can be placed inside a 2n × 2n unitary transformation, up to an overall scaling factor (31). It can also be done more compactly, with two separate m × n devices joined by parts that adjust the phase and the strength of the light (32).

**Fig. 1. How to build any nonunitary transformation.**

The table Tm×n that we want can be placed inside a larger unitary table, SN×N, using matrix dilation (17). Because SN×N can be broken down into simple building blocks, Tm×n can then be pulled out of this light-based circuit.

For any target transformation table, we first use a standard mathematical method called singular value decomposition. It splits the table into three parts, U, D and W. U and W are square tables that keep the number of photons the same, and D is a table with only numbers along its diagonal. Using the same dilation trick, we can build U, D and W in a larger many-way light interference device (the Supplementary Materials give a concrete example).

In this work, we carry out a proof-of-principle experiment that builds the universal 2 × 2 nonunitary transformation. According to Naimark's dilation theorem (26), this 2 × 2 table can be placed inside a 4 × 4 unitary table. As shown in Fig. 2, we use four balanced beam splitters and phase shifters controlled by small time delays. Together they make a four-path complex Hadamard unitary transformation:

S = 1/2 ( −e^(iϕ1)  i e^(iϕ1)  i e^(iϕ2)  e^(iϕ2)
        i e^(iϕ1)  e^(iϕ1)  −e^(iϕ2)  i e^(iϕ2)
        i e^(iϕ1)  e^(iϕ1)  −e^(iϕ2)  i e^(iϕ2)
        −e^(iϕ3)  e^(iϕ3)  i e^(iϕ4)  e^(iϕ4)
        i e^(iϕ3)  −e^(iϕ3)  e^(iϕ4)  −e^(iϕ4) )
    → 1/2 ( −1  i  i  1
             i  1  −1  i
             i  −1  1  i
             1  i  i  −1 )   (1)

Here ϕ1, ϕ2, ϕ3 and ϕ4 are the phase shifts added by the translation stages in each path. A single photon is prepared in a well-defined position, which matches one element of the computational basis. In our experiment, we simply set all the phase shifts to 0. The phase drifts in an unstable way, which limits how well we can control arbitrary phase shifts. So this universal unitary table takes a simpler form.

Which paths we choose as inputs and outputs can then give different unitary and nonunitary transformations. For example, if we take input paths 1 and 3 and output paths 1 and 4, the resulting 2 × 2 table, after scaling, is unitary: T13&14 = 1/2 ( −1  i;  i  1 ). If instead we take input paths 1 and 3 and output paths 1 and 3, the resulting 2 × 2 table is nonunitary: T13&13 = 1/2 ( −1  i;  i  1 ).

We hope that the whole setup could one day be built on a photonic chip, a small chip that guides light. On such a chip, the relative phases between paths would be stable by nature, and built-in phase modulators would let us build unitary and nonunitary transformations on demand and reconfigure them as needed (the Supplementary Materials discuss this further).

**Fig. 2. Our experiment of HOM interference with 2 × 2 unitary and nonunitary transformations.**

These transformations are pulled out of the 4 × 4 unitary table by choosing which input and output ports to use. PBS, polarizing beam splitter; Quartz, compensation crystal; PC, polarizing controller; LP filter, long-pass filter; PPKTP, periodically poled potassium titanyl phosphate crystal; QWP, quarter-wave plate; TS, translation stage; BS, in-fiber beam splitter; PD, single-photon detector.

One built-in difference between unitary and nonunitary devices is their exchange phase. To test whether we can tune the unitary property of the 2 × 2 table T, we use our compact light circuit as the beam splitter in HOM interference. In this way, the interference pattern is set by the exchange phase in the table.

Without loss of generality, we write the table as T ∝ ( t1  r2;  r1  t2 ). The numbers 1 and 2 stand for the two input paths. Each one has a reflection coefficient, r, and a transmission coefficient, t, which describe how much light is sent back or through. We write them as t1/2 = |t1/2| e^(iϕt1/2) and r1/2 = |r1/2| e^(iϕr1/2), where the bars give the size and the phase part gives the phase. The output states then follow from the input states:

â_out = t1 â_in + r2 b̂_in + f â
b̂_out = r1 b̂_in + t2 â_in + f b̂_n   (2)

Here â and b̂ are the operators that create a photon in each path. Following the theory of noisy operators (33), f_a,b is a loss coefficient. The noise operators n̂_a,b may add or remove light, so that the outputs still obey the same basic rules as for any ordinary beam splitter.

We send in pairs of entangled photons, meaning their states are linked. The pair is |Ψ〉 = (|ωs ωi〉 + e^(ϕω) |ωi ωs〉)/2, and the two photons enter the beam splitter from opposite input paths. Applying Eq. 2, the state coming out of the different output ports becomes:

|Ψ〉_out ∝ r1 r2 (|ωs a ωi b〉 + e^(iϕω) |ωi a ωs b〉) + t1 t2 (e^(iϕω) |ωs a ωi b〉 + |ωi a ωs b〉)   (3)

We leave out cases where one or two photons leave through this compact 2 × 2 table. In numbers, the normalized probability of detecting a photon at each of the opposite output ports is:

P(τ) = 1/2 [1 + cos(Δτ + 2ϕpe + ϕω) e^(−σ²τ²)]   (4)

Here τ is the relative time delay we add in the unbalanced HOM interferometer. σ is the RMS bandwidth of a single photon, a measure of how spread out its frequency is. ϕpe = ϕt1 − ϕr1 − ϕr2 + ϕt2 is the exchange phase, and it directly shows whether the 2 × 2 beam splitter is unitary or nonunitary.

Now consider identical photons. If the beam splitter is unitary, with ϕpe = π, the two identical photons arriving at the same time from different input paths bunch together at one output. This is the well-known HOM dip, and it comes directly from the fact that photons are bosons. If the beam splitter is nonunitary, with ϕpe = 0, the same photons instead antibunch, going to opposite outputs. This is the unusual HOM peak, which imitates the behavior of fermions, particles that avoid sharing the same state. So HOM interference gives a visible way to certify whether a transformation table is unitary or nonunitary.

Entangled photons behave differently. If the beam splitter is unitary, antisymmetrically entangled photons, with ϕω = π, give an HOM peak. This comes from both their bosonic nature and the unitary property of the table. In the same way, if the beam splitter is nonunitary, antisymmetrically entangled photons with ϕω = π also give an HOM peak, which again imitates the behavior of fermions. By choosing which input and output paths to use and by tuning the phase shifts, we can therefore build programmable universal nonunitary transformations. This gives a versatile tool for making use of highly tunable quantum interference.

Fig. 2 shows our experiment. Two nonlinear crystals placed one after the other create pairs of photons by spontaneous parametric down conversion, a process in which a laser photon splits into two lower-energy photons. The crystals are turned so that their optical axes are at right angles to each other, which lets us prepare entangled photons with tunable frequency differences. By changing the temperature at which the crystals match the frequencies, we can continuously tune both the frequency difference Δ = |ωs − ωi| and the relative phase ϕω. This gives a flexible way to create the entanglement we want.

The photon pairs enter the 4 × 4 light interference device from different input paths. Single-photon detectors labeled A, B, C and D record the photons at the four output ports. We then study the coincidence events, where two detectors click at the same time, using every pair of detectors (AB, AC, AD, BC, BD and CD). With all the time delays set to zero, our experiment readily produces the table S0. More complex 4 × 4 tables can also be made by stabilizing and shifting the phases.

Because we only create photon pairs, we choose two random input paths and two random output paths. This gives a compact 2 × 2 table. For example, input paths 1-in and 3-in with output paths 1-out and 3-out would give the table T13&14 = 1/2 ( −e^(iϕ1)  i e^(iϕ3);  i e^(iϕ2)  e^(iϕ4) ).

By scanning the relative time delay precisely, we can directly watch how the two-photon interference pattern changes over time, as shown in Figs. 3 to 5. Fitting our results to the prediction in Eq. 4 gives the frequency differences in Figs. 4 and 5 as Δ = 2.2 THz and Δ = 4.2 THz, respectively.

For identical photons, the HOM pattern is a dip or a peak within the coherence time, the window over which the photons stay in step with each other. Whether we see a dip or a peak depends on the unitary property of the 2 × 2 table we pulled out. Because choosing different input and output paths gives different unitary properties, the interference patterns can look completely different, as Fig. 3 shows.

For symmetrically and antisymmetrically entangled photons, the HOM pattern instead rises and falls in a regular wave within the coherence time. Whether the pattern has a dip or a peak at zero delay depends on two things: the symmetry of the incoming entangled photons and the unitary property of the 2 × 2 table. So the table that comes from different input and output paths has a tunable unitary property, and its interference patterns show the matching patterns. Because the incoming entangled photons are symmetric, the dip and peak in Fig. 4 look like those in Fig. 3, while the dip and peak in Fig. 5 are the opposite of those in Fig. 3.

**Fig. 3. HOM interference of identical photons with the 4 × 4 light interference device.**

The input paths are (A) 1-in and 2-in, (B) 1-in and 3-in, (C) 1-in and 4-in, (D) 2-in and 3-in, (E) 2-in and 4-in, and (F) 3-in and 4-in.

**Fig. 4. HOM interference of antisymmetrically entangled photons with the 4 × 4 light interference device, with frequency difference Δ = 2.2 THz.**

The input paths are (A) 1-in and 2-in, (B) 1-in and 3-in, (C) 1-in and 4-in, (D) 2-in and 3-in, (E) 2-in and 4-in, and (F) 3-in and 4-in.

**Fig. 5. HOM interference of symmetrically entangled photons with the 4 × 4 light interference device, with frequency difference Δ = 4.2 THz.**

The input paths are (A) 1-in and 2-in, (B) 1-in and 3-in, (C) 1-in and 4-in, (D) 2-in and 3-in, (E) 2-in and 4-in, and (F) 3-in and 4-in.

This simple but efficient method, based on ordinary beam splitters and phase shifters, lets us measure how clear each HOM pattern is. We describe this with the visibility, which runs from 0 (no pattern) to 1 (a perfect pattern). Fig. 6 shows the visibility of every pattern we measured. On average, the visibility reaches 0.80 ± 0.02 for identical photons with the same frequency, 0.83 ± 0.04 for symmetrically entangled photons, and 0.81 ± 0.04 for antisymmetrically entangled photons. Building the many-way device on a photonic chip could raise these values further.

Some existing schemes can make a nonunitary 2 × 2 table that relies on lost light. But because the transformation is lossy and nonunitary, far fewer coincidence events are recorded, which is completely different from a lossless unitary transformation. This would seriously limit their use in quantum simulation and quantum computing. Our scheme avoids this problem by using unitary and nonunitary transformations that are lossy. As a result, the number of coincidence events we measured stays almost the same. Small differences come from the different efficiencies of the single-photon detectors and the fiber couplings.

**Fig. 6. Visibility of HOM interference with the 4 × 4 light interference device.**

The measured visibilities of the patterns in (A) Fig. 3, (B) Fig. 4 and (C) Fig. 5. Here (i, j) stand for input ports i-in and j-in, as shown in Fig. 2.

Our four-input, four-output device also allows interference of three and four photons. The resulting quantum state can be tuned continuously by using photon loss, relative phase, and the choice of input and output paths. For example, suppose four indistinguishable photons arrive at the same time at the four input paths. The 4 × 4 table in Eq. 7 then turns the state into:

|Ψ〉 = [ e^(2i(ϕ1+ϕ3)) (6|4000〉 + 6|0400〉 + 2|2200〉)
      + e^(2i(ϕ2+ϕ4)) (6|0040〉 + 6|0004〉 + 2|0022〉)
      − (e^(2i(ϕ1+ϕ4)) + e^(2i(ϕ2+ϕ3))) (|2002〉 − |2020〉 − |0220〉 + |0202〉 + 2|1111〉)
      − 2i (e^(2i(ϕ2+ϕ3)) − e^(2i(ϕ1+ϕ4))) (|2011〉 + |0211〉 + |1102〉 + |1120〉) ] / 8

Here i, j, k and l are the symmetric superpositions of the four-photon states in which (i, j, k, l) photons leave through the four output ports. When ϕ1 = ϕ2 = ϕ3 = ϕ4 = 0, the four-photon state simplifies to |Ψ〉 → 6(|4000〉 + |0400〉 + |0040〉 + |0004〉)/8 + (|2200〉 + |2020〉 + |2002〉 + |0220〉 + |0202〉 + |0022〉 + |1111〉)/4. When instead ϕ1 = π/2 and ϕ2 = ϕ3 = ϕ4 = 0, it simplifies to |Ψ〉 → 6(|4000〉 + |0400〉 − |0040〉 − |0004〉 + 2|2200〉 − 2|0022〉)/8 + 2i(|2011〉 − |0211〉 − |1120〉 + |1102〉)/4.

These results show ordinary many-photon interference based on a high-dimensional unitary transformation. To see unusual many-photon interference based on a high-dimensional nonunitary transformation, we would need a larger many-way light interference device. Our experiment shows the universal nonunitary transformation for photon pairs. The overall scheme could be extended to many-photon interference, so that any target high-dimensional unitary or nonunitary table can be built on demand.
parts.discussion:
## Discussion

We take any nonunitary transformation table, of any size m × n, and place it inside a larger unitary table. This gives a short but efficient way to handle any kind of m × n nonunitary transformation. Because we can choose which input and output paths to use, we can control whether the transformation behaves in a unitary way or not. Along with this comes a hidden exchange phase, a sign that changes when the two photons swap places.

To check this surprising quantum effect, we ran a Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference experiment to watch how the photons behave when they swap places. With the usual unitary devices, two identical photons, and two photons that are "symmetrically" entangled, both give the usual HOM dip. A dip means the two photons come out together at one output, so the detectors at the two outputs rarely click at the same time. Two photons that are "antisymmetrically" entangled give the usual HOM peak instead, where the detectors at the two outputs click together more often. These are the well-known HOM patterns, and they come directly from the fact that photons are bosons.

With nonunitary devices, the pattern flips. Two identical photons, and two symmetrically entangled photons, now give the HOM peak. Antisymmetrically entangled photons give the HOM dip. These are unusual HOM patterns that imitate the behaviour of fermions, a type of particle that avoids sharing the same state.

It is worth stressing that, in many-way light interference, the way photons affect each other can be tuned. This has great potential for building new functions and complex quantum gates (the basic building blocks of quantum computers) in integrated photonic circuits, which are small chips that guide light. It matters most for tasks that can be programmed, such as quantum simulation and quantum computing.

A nonunitary transformation caused by lost light naturally describes how an open physical system, one that can exchange energy or particles with its surroundings, interacts with the rest of the world. It may be linked to non-Hermitian systems, which are systems that are not closed and can lose energy. This could open new paths for quantum emulation, where one system imitates another, and for extremely sensitive measurements.

Finally, being able to carry out any m × n nonunitary transformation gives us a chance to handle quantum information carried by many photons at once and by many different light paths at once. This would bring great benefits from bringing advanced nonunitary devices into integrated quantum optics, and it paves the way toward large-scale, programmable platforms for quantum information.
